```{r load-lib, include = FALSE}
library(tidyverse)
library(tidymodels)
library(learningtower)
library(haven)

```


```{r load-data, include=FALSE}
# load your data here and any pre-processing/cleaning 
# Load data set
student_math <- read_rds("data/student_math.rds")

# Remove unnecessary columns and missing mathematics scores
student_math_pro <- student_math |>
  select(-general_family_support) |>
  filter(
    if_all(
      starts_with("math_score_pv"),
      ~ !is.na(.)
    )
  )

# Select variables for the investigation
student_processed <- student_math_pro |>
  select(
    student_id,
    country_code,
    student_age,
    student_gender,
    family_socioeconomic_status,
    family_support,
    home_possessions_index,
    home_ict_resources,
    highest_parental_education,
    parental_education_years,
    highest_parental_occupational_status,
    starts_with("math_score_pv")
  )

# Calculate mean mathematics score
student_processed <- student_processed |>
  mutate(
    math_score = rowMeans(
      across(starts_with("math_score_pv"))
    )
  ) |>
  select(-starts_with("math_score_pv"))

# Calculate statistics
score_stats <- student_processed %>%
  filter(!is.na(math_score)) %>%
  summarise(
    mean_score = mean(math_score),
    median_score = median(math_score),
    q1 = quantile(math_score, 0.25),
    q3 = quantile(math_score, 0.75)
  )

```


## Research Question

Describe your research question here. Include why this question might be of interest. 

**Question**: 
*How are parental education, parental occupational status, and home ICT resources associated with students’ mathematics performance in PISA 2025?*

**Why**:
*Students' home environments may play an important role in their educational outcomes. Differences in parental education, occupational status, and access to ICT resources may be associated with students' opportunities to learn and their mathematics performance. Investigating these relationships can help us better understand how family background relates to educational achievement.*


## Data

Briefly describe your dataset here - include a description of the key variables you will be investigating. 
Include a citation for your data. 
See http://libraryguides.vu.edu.au/c.php?g=386501&p=4347840 for guidance on proper citation for datasets.

### Dataset overview

*This investigation uses student-level data from the PISA 2025 Student Questionnaire, published by the Organisation for Economic Co-operation and Development (OECD). The dataset contains information on students' backgrounds and mathematics performance, allowing us to investigate the associations between family circumstances and academic achievement (OECD, n.d.).*

### Key variables

Our investigation focuses on three main factors that may be related to students' mathematics performance.

Mathematics performance: math_score represents each student's mathematics performance.

Parental education: We use parental_education_years to show the number of years of education completed by parents. We also kept highest_parental_education in the dataset.

Parental occupational status: We use highest_parental_occupational_status to examine whether parents' occupational status is related to students' mathematics performance.

Home ICT resources: We use home_ict_resources to represent the ICT resources available at home.

Other variables, such as student age, gender, country, family socioeconomic status and home possessions, were also kept to provide more information about students' backgrounds.

### Data processing

Our starting material came in two parts: the PISA 2025 data file and the student questionnaire. We worked from the data file only, so the questionnaire was set aside and everything below is based on the 755,721 student rows in `student_math`.

We first used `summary()` in R to check the data and identify missing values. Mathematics scores were missing for two countries, so we excluded them: Uzbekistan (all of its records) and Belgium (one record). That took out 8,653 records, leaving 747,068 students.

To make the data easier to use, we calculated the average of the ten mathematics scores for each student using `rowMeans()`. We created a new variable called `math_score` and then removed the original ten score columns.

We then selected the variables needed for our research: mathematics scores, parental education, parental occupational status and home ICT resources.

We did not remove all missing values from the other variables at this stage. Instead, we excluded missing observations when needed for individual visualisations and analyses, so that each analysis kept as many students as its own variables allowed, rather than losing rows it did not use.

The table sets the processed data against the original file: `student_math` (755,721 rows, 24 variables) and `student_processed` (747,068 rows, 12 variables, after irrelevant variables were dropped and the ten plausible values became one `math_score`).

### Data citation
The dataset was retrieved on 28 October 2026 from the OECD PISA 2025 database: https://webfs.oecd.org/pisa2022/index.html.

## Analysis

Of the 755,721 students included in the questionnaire dataset, 747,068 remained after removing those whose mathematics scores were missing. In turn, this dropped the number of represented countries in the dataset from 90 to 89, as Uzbekistan ('UZB')'s mathematics scores are completely missing. According to the official results report, both mathematics and reading scores were omitted for Uzbekistan due to "a number of inconsistencies ... that require further investigation" (OECD, 2026). These account for 8562 of the removed rows, and the remaining one corresponds to a Belgian ('BEL') student whose mathematics scores are also missing (Student ID 05608066).

As a preliminary analysis, we used the processed dataset to visualize the distribution of students' mathematics scores, as seen in Figure 1.

### **Figure 1**

```{r echo=FALSE}
# Calculate the 2.5th and 97.5th percentiles
ci <- quantile(
  student_processed$math_score,
  probs = c(0.025, 0.975)
)

ggplot(student_processed, aes(x = math_score)) +
  geom_histogram(
    bins = 50,
    fill = "steelblue",
    color = "white"
  ) +
  geom_vline(
    xintercept = ci,
    color = "#D98282",
    linetype = "dashed",
    linewidth = 1
  ) +
  annotate(
    "text",
    x = ci[1],
    y = Inf,
    label = paste0("2.5%: ", round(ci[1], 2)),
    color = "#D98282",
    vjust = 1.5,
    size = 3.5
  ) +
  annotate(
    "text",
    x = ci[2],
    y = Inf,
    label = paste0("97.5%: ", round(ci[2], 2)),
    color = "#D98282",
    vjust = 1.5,
    size = 3.5
  ) +
  labs(
    title = "Distribution of Mathematics Scores",
    subtitle = "Central 95% of Mathematics Scores | PISA 2025",
    x = "Mathematics Score",
    y = "Number of Students"
  ) +
  theme_minimal()
```

*Note.* This figure is a frequency histogram showing the distribution of mathematics scores across the PISA 2025 dataset.




From the histogram in Figure 1, we observed a unimodal distribution of mathematics scores across students, with a noticeably strong right skew. This shows that most of the data points (ie., individual students' mathematics scores) were below the mean, which is reflected by the mean (`r score_stats$mean_score %>% sprintf(fmt='%.2f')`) being greater than the median (`r score_stats$median_score %>% sprintf(fmt='%.2f')`). 

After analyzing the overall data, we moved on to explore the individual variables' relationship with mathematics score, starting with parental education (measured as the highest number of years of education attained by either parent). This data was divided into five levels (6, 9, 12, 14, 16) in PISA 2025, determined using the ISCED international standard (OECD, 2026).

Figure 2 shows a visualization of distribution of mathematics scores across these five groups. The plot suggests a possible positive correlation between students' mathematics scores and parental education years.

### **Figure 2**

```{r parental_education, echo=FALSE}
#the relationship between parental education years and mathematics score
# Prepare data
education_data <- student_processed %>%
  drop_na(parental_education_years,
    math_score) %>%
  mutate(
    parental_education = factor(
      as.numeric(parental_education_years)
    )
  )


# Violin plot
ggplot(
    education_data,
    aes(
        x = parental_education,
        y = math_score
    )
) +
    geom_violin(
        trim = TRUE,
        fill = "#DCD6F7",
        colour = "#7566A8",
        alpha = 0.8
    ) +
    geom_boxplot(
        width = 0.12,
        outlier.shape = NA,
        fill = "white",
        colour = "#493A70",
        linewidth = 0.5
    ) +
    labs(
        title = "Parental Education and Mathematics Performance",
        subtitle = "PISA 2025 Student Data",
        x = "Highest Education of Parents in Years",
        y = "Mathematics Score"
    ) +
    coord_flip() +
    theme_minimal()
```

*Note.* This figure is a violin plot combined with boxplots, showing the distribution of mathematics scores for each level of highest parental education, in the PISA 2025 dataset.




The next variable analyzed in relation to mathematics performance was highest parental occupational status, visualized as a hexagonal bin plot with a linear regression line in Figure 3. Similarly to the parental education analysis, we observed an apparent positive correlation with mathematics performance.

### **Figure 3**

```{r main2, echo=FALSE}
#the relationship between highest parental occupational status and mathematics scores
student_processed|>
filter(
    !is.na(highest_parental_occupational_status)
  ) |>
ggplot(
  aes(
    x = highest_parental_occupational_status,
    y = math_score
  )
) +
  geom_hex(bins = 100) +
  scale_fill_gradientn(
  colours = c(
    "#E2E3FF",
    "#5968E8",
    "#1049F8",
    "#171D85"
  ),
  trans = "log10",
  name = "Number of students"
) +
    geom_smooth(
  method = "lm",
  formula = y ~ x,
  colour = "#C065EE",
  linewidth = 1,
  se = TRUE
)+
  labs(
    title = "Parental Occupational Status and Mathematics Achievement",
    x = "Family Highest Occupational grade",
    y = "Mathematics score"
  ) +
  theme_minimal()
```

*Note.* This figure is a hexagon bin plot with a simple least-squares linear regression line added, showing the distribution of mathematics scores across family highest occupational grade in the PISA 2025 dataset. Note that the color for number of students is base-10 logarithmic.



The third variable we explored was home ICT resources, representing the relative amount of access each student has to information and communications technology resources at home (OECD, 2026). We visualized the relationship between home ICT resources and mathematics performance via a binned scatterplot, as seen in Figure 4. Here, the trend is more complex, as depicted via the generalized additive model (GAM) smoothing line, and there appears to be a peak of some sort between the values of 0 and 1.5 for home ICT resources index.

### **Figure 4**

```{r main3, echo=FALSE}
#the relationship between ICT and mathematics score
clean_data <- student_processed |>
     filter(
         is.finite(home_ict_resources)
     ) 
 ggplot(
    clean_data,
    aes(x = home_ict_resources, y = math_score)
) +
    
    stat_summary_bin(
        fun = mean,
        bins = 1000,
        geom = "point",
        colour = "#F2A6B3",
        size = 1
    ) +
    geom_smooth(
    method = "gam",
    colour = "skyblue",
    linewidth = 1.1
)+
    labs(
        title = "Home ICT Resources and Mathematics score",
        x = "Home ICT Resources Index",
        y = "Mean Mathematics score in each class"
    ) +
    theme_minimal()

```

*Note.* This figure shows a binned scatter plot (mean mathematics score plotted for each of 1000 home ICT resources index bins) with a GAM smoothing line shown in blue.



### Limitations

The most significant limitation of the data across variables was its student-reported nature: for example, students were expected to report their parents' highest level of education. However, past studies conducted on previous iterations of PISA, in which parents were also asked to report their education levels (this was not a part of the 2025 questionnaires), found large discrepancies between student and parents' responses (Jerrim et al., 2024).
